table.title: [val2][adversarial] Incident IDs vs prose
table.md:
| Incident | Trace ID | Severity | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| INC-20240611-0042 | 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736 | P1 | Checkout latency spiked to eight seconds after the cache cluster failed over to the secondary region. |
| INC-20240611-0043 | 00f067aa0ba902b7 | P3 | Typo in the Spanish translation of the password reset email. |
| INC-20240612-0001 | 7d3e0a1b9c2f4e6d | P2 | Webhook retries exhausted for one merchant. |

understanding.purpose: Connect each incident and its trace identifier to a severity and a brief description of the problem.
understanding.reading: Readers can scan severity and summary for incidents of interest, then use the incident and trace IDs to locate or investigate a specific record.
groups: Incident and Trace ID identify the same record and support lookup.
Severity and Summary describe the incident and support triage.
keep_intact: Trace IDs should remain intact where possible, since they are long, unbroken identifiers.
Incident IDs should remain intact where possible so they are easy to recognize and copy.
Severity codes should remain on one line.
may_wrap: Summary prose can wrap naturally between words; its line count will largely determine row height.
Incident IDs can wrap at hyphens if more space is needed for summaries.
Trace IDs may require forced breaking in a prose-first design.

preferred.name: r1A
preferred.note: Keep the strongest intact-identifier arrangement as the reference: both lookup columns fit on one line, while summary wraps naturally.

preferred.name: r3A
preferred.note: Give Incident the 148px needed to keep its IDs on one line, taking 18px from Summary. Both identifying columns and severity remain intact, while summaries retain room to wrap.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Keep trace IDs intact and move 18px from Incident to Summary. This tests whether allowing incident IDs to wrap at hyphens produces a useful improvement in prose rhythm while preserving trace lookup.

bad.name: r0C
bad.note: Give summaries substantially more room while keeping incident IDs intact, accepting forced breaks in long trace IDs.
bad.why: The long trace ID splits inside the identifier, making it harder to scan or copy accurately.

bad.name: r1B
bad.note: Give summary more space than r0A while retaining more trace width than r0C. This tests whether a smaller forced split in the longest trace buys a useful reduction in prose wrapping.
bad.why: The long trace ID splits inside the identifier without reducing the table's height.

bad.name: r1C
bad.note: Allow incident IDs to wrap at hyphens and split the longest trace, giving summary nearly as much width as r0C. This tests a prose-first alternative with a wider trace column.
bad.why: The trace ID splits inside the identifier, and every incident ID wraps onto two lines.

bad.name: r3B
bad.note: Accept wrapping incident IDs at hyphens to give summaries 20px more width than r2A. Trace IDs and severity codes remain intact; compare whether the prose gains enough to justify the broken incident IDs.
bad.why: Every incident ID breaks across three lines, weakening row scanning and making the table substantially taller.

bad.name: r3C
bad.note: Keep incident IDs intact and give the prose more room by narrowing Trace ID. The longest trace will require a forced break, so this explores whether improved summary flow is worth the cost to identifier scanning and copying.
bad.why: Like r1B, it splits the long trace ID without reducing the table's height.

rationale: r1A and r3A are identical: both keep the incident and trace IDs intact while giving the summaries enough room to read in short phrases. Severity is compact, and all headers remain on one line. r2A preserves the trace IDs but wraps every incident ID, making the first column less convenient to scan.

general: Give identifiers enough width to remain intact when readers need to scan or copy them.
Allocate width according to each column's role and wrapping behavior, rather than making columns equal.
Judge row height alongside readability; a shorter table can be worse if it breaks important content.
specific: The longest trace ID needs 266 px including padding and border to stay on one line.
The incident IDs need 148 px to stay on one line, while Severity fits at 73 px.
The remaining 247 px gives the summaries usable line lengths within the 734 px width limit.

tradeoffs: Widening Summary gives prose more room but requires either breaking the long trace ID or wrapping incident IDs. r2A makes the latter trade and remains publishable, though its incident column is less scannable.
uncertain: The ranges are conservative estimates, not tested thresholds; changes must still total no more than 734 px. Designers may disagree on how costly wrapping incident IDs is compared with giving summaries more width.

critique.good: Both identifiers remain intact, severity is easy to scan, and the prose wraps at word boundaries. The rows read clearly as units.
critique.problems: The first summary takes three lines and the other two take two lines. The trace column leaves substantial empty space on the shorter IDs, while the summary feels comparatively constrained.
critique.cause: The 266px trace column is needed to hold the longest trace on one line; together with the 148px incident and 73px severity columns, it leaves 247px for summary.

critique.good: All trace IDs remain intact, and the wider summary column gives the prose a little more room without increasing table height.
critique.problems: Every incident ID wraps at a hyphen, weakening the column's scan rhythm and making the identifiers harder to recognize and copy visually. The extra summary width does not reduce any row's line count compared with r0A.
critique.cause: The 130px incident column provides only 109px of text space, less than the 127px needed for the full ID. Moving those 18px to summary does not reach a useful wrapping threshold.

critique.good: The wider summary is more comfortable to read and brings the last row down to one line. Incident IDs and severity codes stay intact.
critique.problems: The longest trace ID splits within the identifier, making it harder to follow and transcribe. The wide summary also leaves more unused space in the shorter rows.
critique.cause: The 200px trace column provides 179px of text space, well below the 245px needed for the longest trace. Its saved width goes to the 313px summary column.

critique.good: Both identifiers and all severity codes stay intact. The columns have clear roles, and each row reads as a coherent incident. The summaries wrap naturally without making the table taller than the alternatives.
critique.problems: The summary column is relatively narrow, so the first description occupies three lines and the others occupy two.
critique.cause: The 266px Trace ID column preserves the longest identifier, while the 148px Incident and 73px Severity columns preserve their contents; together they leave 247px for Summary.

critique.good: The wider summary column gives the prose more room, while incident IDs and severity codes remain on one line.
critique.problems: The longest trace ID splits across lines, making it harder to scan and copy. The extra summary width does not reduce the table height.
critique.cause: Reducing Trace ID to 220px leaves 199px for text, less than the 245px needed by the longest identifier.

critique.good: The summary column is the widest of the three designs, and the last summary fits on one line. Severity remains easy to scan.
critique.problems: Every incident ID wraps, and the longest trace ID also splits. The broken identifiers make rows harder to scan without reducing the overall table height.
critique.cause: The 130px Incident column leaves 109px for text, less than its 127px one-line requirement; the 220px Trace ID column also cannot contain the longest trace.

critique.good: The trace IDs and severity codes remain intact, and the headers are clear. The summary has enough width for natural word wrapping, with no mid-word splits. Borders make the records easy to follow across the table.
critique.problems: Every incident ID wraps onto a second line, separating its final digits from the rest of the identifier. The first summary takes three lines, making that row noticeably taller than the others.
critique.cause: The 130px Incident column provides 109px of text space, short of the 127px needed for a complete ID. The 265px Summary column provides 244px for prose; the long first description therefore wraps to three lines.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

ref_equal.why: Severity takes as much space as the longer fields, leaving the summary narrow and forcing the longest trace ID to break.

ref_auto.why: The trace IDs stay intact and the summaries read well, but every incident ID breaks across three lines, making identification and comparison difficult.

r2A.why: Trace IDs stay intact and the summaries have reasonable room, but every incident ID breaks across two lines.

r1A.why: Both identifier columns stay intact, severity has sufficient space, and the summaries wrap into manageable lines with consistent row rhythm.

r0C.why: Incident IDs stay intact and the summaries have generous space, but the longest trace ID breaks across two lines.

raw.unsure: The trade-off between preserving the longest trace ID and giving the summaries more space is close; D keeps both identifier types intact while retaining readable summaries.

r1A.why: Both identifiers stay intact, severity is compact, and the summaries wrap naturally into readable row units.

ref_auto.why: Incident IDs break across three lines, making them hard to scan and compare, despite the readable summaries and intact trace IDs.

r2A.why: Trace IDs stay intact and summaries read well, but every incident ID splits across two lines.

r0C.why: Incident IDs stay intact and the summaries have comfortable space, but the longest trace ID breaks across lines.

ref_equal.why: The oversized severity column takes space from both the trace IDs and summaries; the longest trace ID splits and the prose wraps into narrow, tall blocks.

raw.unsure: The trace IDs are small in the image, but the longest appears intact in A and split in D and E.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
